questions.stem: Which of the following joints is a syndesmosis?
options: Attachment of the teeth to their sockets
questions.explanation: A syndesmosis is a fibrous joint in which bones are joined by a ligament or membrane: the distal tibiofibular joint and the interosseous membranes of the forearm and leg are examples. The pubic symphysis is fibrocartilaginous, the 1st sternocostal joint a synchondrosis, the tooth–socket union a gomphosis, and sutures are fibrous joints peculiar to the skull.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a saddle (sellar) synovial joint?
questions.explanation: In saddle joints both surfaces are concave in one direction and convex in the other; they allow movement about two axes, including opposition. Examples: the 1st carpometacarpal joint and the sternoclavicular joint. The radiocarpal joint is ellipsoid, the humero-ulnar a hinge, the proximal radio-ulnar a pivot and the acromioclavicular a plane joint.

questions.stem: Which of the following pairings is WRONG?
questions.explanation: The atlanto-occipital joint is ellipsoid (condylar) and allows the 'yes' movement. Pivot joints are the median atlanto-axial joint ('no' movement) and the proximal and distal radio-ulnar joints.

questions.stem: The growth plate (epiphyseal plate) is an example of which type of joint?
questions.explanation: In primary cartilaginous joints (synchondroses) bones are joined by hyaline cartilage and most ossify with time: the epiphyseal plate, the 1st rib–manubrium joint, the spheno-occipital synchondrosis. Secondary cartilaginous joints (symphyses) contain fibrocartilage and lie in the midline.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: Which of the following about the temporomandibular joint is FALSE?
options: Part of the lateral pterygoid attaches to the disc.
On opening the mouth, the condyle and disc glide forwards towards the articular tubercle.
The articular disc divides the joint into upper and lower cavities.
The articular surfaces are covered with hyaline cartilage.
Hinge (rotation) movement occurs in the lower joint cavity.
questions.explanation: The articular surfaces of the TMJ are covered with fibrocartilage, not hyaline cartilage (related to the intramembranous origin of the bones). The disc divides the joint in two: rotation occurs in the lower cavity, forward gliding (translation) in the upper. Lateral pterygoid pulls the condyle and disc forwards.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: A patient who yawned cannot close the mouth. The mandibular condyle has passed in front of the articular tubercle. In which direction is the jaw pushed for reduction?
questions.explanation: TMJ dislocation is almost always anterior; the condyle catches in front of the eminence and spasm of the muscles (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid) holds it there. With the thumbs on the lower molars the jaw is pushed first downwards (to pass beneath the eminence) and then backwards.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: The gelatinous centre of the intervertebral disc (nucleus pulposus) is embryologically a remnant of what?
questions.explanation: The nucleus pulposus is a remnant of the notochord; the surrounding anulus fibrosus consists of fibrocartilaginous rings of sclerotomal origin. With age its water content falls and disc height decreases.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: Why are lumbar disc herniations most often posterolateral?
options: The anterior longitudinal ligament supports the back.
The anulus fibrosus is thicker posteriorly.
The posterior longitudinal ligament is thick in the midline and thin at the sides.
The nucleus pulposus lies near the front of the disc.
The ligamentum flavum pushes the disc from the sides.
questions.explanation: The posterior longitudinal ligament is a narrow band behind the vertebral bodies and supports the disc only in the midline. The anulus fibrosus is also thinner posteriorly. So the nucleus pulposus herniates most often posterolaterally and compresses the nerve root.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: Which yellow ligament, rich in elastic fibres, runs between the laminae of the vertebral arches?
questions.explanation: The ligamenta flava join adjacent laminae; thanks to their elastic fibres they help straighten the spine after flexion. In lumbar puncture the needle passes the skin, supraspinous and interspinous ligaments and then the ligamentum flavum (a 'pop') to reach the epidural space.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: At which joint does most of the 'no' movement (rotation) of the head occur?
questions.explanation: At the atlanto-axial joints (one median pivot and two lateral plane joints) the atlas rotates around the dens; about half of neck rotation occurs here. The 'yes' movement is at the atlanto-occipital joint. The alar ligaments limit excessive rotation.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: Which joint does the head of a rib form with the bodies of two adjacent thoracic vertebrae?
options: Joint of the head of the rib
questions.explanation: The head of a typical rib forms the joint of the head of the rib with the demifacets on the bodies of two adjacent vertebrae and the intervening disc; its tubercle forms the costotransverse joint with the transverse process of the lower vertebra. These two joints allow the rib's 'bucket-handle' and 'pump-handle' movements in breathing.

questions.stem: Which is the only true (synovial) joint connecting the upper limb to the axial skeleton?
questions.explanation: The only articular connection between the upper limb and the axial skeleton is the sternoclavicular joint. It is a saddle joint with an articular disc and very strong support from the costoclavicular ligament; so it rarely dislocates, and clavicle fracture is more common. The scapulothoracic 'joint' is not a true joint.

questions.stem: A rugby player who fell on his shoulder has a step between the acromion and clavicle, with the outer end of the clavicle prominent above. Which ligament must also be torn for this (type III) separation?
questions.explanation: In acromioclavicular separation, if only the AC ligament tears the step is slight. If the coracoclavicular ligament (conoid and trapezoid parts) also tears, the scapula and arm drop and the end of the clavicle stays markedly high.

questions.stem: A volleyball player falls with the arm abducted and externally rotated. A shoulder dislocation is found, and after reduction there is sensory loss over the outer shoulder. What is the direction of the dislocation and which nerve is injured?
questions.explanation: The glenohumeral joint is the most frequently dislocated large joint in the body; more than 95% of dislocations are anteroinferior because the lower part of the capsule is weakest. As the humeral head descends, the axillary nerve just below the surgical neck is stretched.

questions.stem: Which fibrocartilaginous ring deepens the glenohumeral joint?
questions.explanation: The glenoid cavity is shallow; the glenoid labrum around it deepens the socket. The long head of biceps attaches to its upper part; a tear there is a SLAP lesion, and a tear of the anteroinferior part a Bankart lesion.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old painter has pain between 60° and 120° when raising the arm sideways (painful arc). Which rotator cuff tendon is impinged under the acromion and torn most often?
questions.explanation: The supraspinatus tendon passes through the narrow space between the acromion, coraco-acromial ligament and humeral head. It is impinged in the mid-range of abduction (subacromial impingement); degeneration and tears are most common in this tendon, in its poorly vascularised zone.

questions.stem: Why does the 'carrying angle' of the elbow exist?
options: The radial head is longer than the ulna
The medial edge of the trochlea lies lower than the lateral edge
The radial collateral ligament is short
The capitulum of the humerus is large
questions.explanation: In extension the forearm angles outwards relative to the arm (~10° in men, ~15° in women). This is because the medial lip of the trochlea extends further down. Cubitus valgus and varus are an increase and decrease of this angle.

questions.stem: Which of the following about the elbow joint is FALSE?
options: The ulnar collateral ligament protects against valgus stress.
The humero-ulnar joint is a hinge joint.
The anular ligament encircles the radial head.
Both flexion and rotation occur at the humeroradial joint.
The proximal radio-ulnar joint has a separate joint capsule.
questions.explanation: The elbow is a compound joint of the humero-ulnar, humeroradial and proximal radio-ulnar joints, all three within a single capsule. The medial (ulnar) collateral ligament protects against valgus stress, the lateral (radial) collateral ligament against varus stress.

questions.stem: At which joints do pronation and supination occur?
questions.explanation: In pronation–supination the radius rotates proximally within the radial notch of the ulna and distally around the head of the ulna. The two pivot joints work together with the interosseous membrane.

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT directly take part in the radiocarpal joint?
options: Distal articular surface of the radius
questions.explanation: The radiocarpal joint is formed proximally by the radius and the triangular fibrocartilage disc (TFCC) and distally by the scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum. The ulna is separated from the carpal bones by the disc, so it does not enter the joint directly.

questions.stem: What type of joint are the metacarpophalangeal joints?
questions.explanation: MCP joints are ellipsoid: flexion–extension and abduction–adduction occur, with no active rotation. The interphalangeal joints are pure hinge joints.

questions.stem: Which ligament, known as the strongest in the body, prevents hyperextension of the hip?
options: Ligament of the head of the femur
questions.explanation: The inverted-Y iliofemoral ligament (Bigelow's ligament) runs between the AIIS and the intertrochanteric line. When standing it passively stops the trunk falling backwards, allowing upright posture without muscular effort.

questions.stem: In a traffic accident a driver's knee struck the dashboard; the leg is shortened, flexed, adducted and internally rotated. A hip dislocation is found. Which nerve is most often injured in this dislocation?
questions.explanation: In a 'dashboard' injury with the knee bent, the femoral head dislocates posteriorly (most hip dislocations). Behind, the head compresses or stretches the sciatic nerve; the fibular part is most often affected.

questions.stem: The artery running within the ligament of the head of the femur is usually a branch of which artery?
questions.explanation: The artery of the ligament of the head (acetabular artery) is a branch of the obturator artery; in childhood it makes an important contribution to the femoral head, in adults only a small one. In adults the head is mainly supplied by the medial circumflex femoral artery.

questions.stem: A footballer hears a 'pop' from his knee while changing direction suddenly, and the knee swells rapidly. On examination, with the knee at 90° of flexion, the tibia slides excessively forwards. Which structure is injured?
questions.explanation: The anterior cruciate ligament prevents the tibia sliding forwards on the femur; the anterior drawer and Lachman tests are positive. The posterior cruciate ligament prevents it sliding backwards (posterior drawer test).

questions.stem: What is the main reason the medial meniscus tears more often than the lateral meniscus?
options: It is firmly attached to the tibial collateral ligament and so is less mobile
It is attached to the popliteus tendon
It has no blood supply at all
It is fused with the posterior cruciate ligament
It is smaller and more circular
questions.explanation: The medial meniscus is C-shaped and its outer edge is attached to the medial collateral ligament; because it cannot move during movement, it tears. The lateral meniscus is more circular and mobile; the popliteus tendon separates it from the collateral ligament. 'Unhappy triad': MCL + ACL + medial meniscus.

questions.stem: Which muscle unlocks the knee, locked in full extension, so that flexion can begin?
questions.explanation: In the last degrees of full extension the femur rotates medially on the tibia and the knee locks. At the start of flexion popliteus unlocks it by rotating the femur laterally (or, when not weight-bearing, the tibia medially).

questions.stem: In a valgus stress caused by a blow to the outer side of the knee, which ligament is damaged first?
questions.explanation: A force from the outside stretches the medial side of the knee (valgus): the medial collateral ligament tears, and in severe injuries the ACL and medial meniscus are also involved. The lateral collateral ligament is injured in varus stress.

questions.stem: A young woman who rolled her ankle inwards on uneven ground has swelling and tenderness in front of the lateral malleolus. Which ligament is most often injured?
questions.explanation: Most ankle sprains occur in plantarflexion and inversion; the anterior talofibular ligament, the weakest lateral ligament, tears first, followed by the calcaneofibular ligament. The medial deltoid ligament is very strong and is usually injured together with a malleolar fracture.

questions.stem: At which joints do inversion and eversion of the foot mainly occur?
questions.explanation: The talocrural joint is a hinge and allows dorsiflexion–plantarflexion. Inversion–eversion occurs below the talus, at the subtalar (talocalcaneal) and talocalcaneonavicular joints, with a small part at the transverse tarsal (Chopart) joint.

questions.stem: In which position is the ankle (talocrural) joint most stable, and why?
options: In inversion, because the lateral ligaments are taut.
In dorsiflexion, because the trochlea of the talus is wider in front and locks firmly between the malleoli.
In plantarflexion, because the deltoid ligament is tautest.
In plantarflexion, because the malleoli fully grip the talus.
In neutral, because the capsule is most lax.
questions.explanation: The trochlea of the talus is wide in front and narrow behind. In dorsiflexion the wide front part wedges between the malleoli and the joint is stable. In plantarflexion the narrow part lies in the mortise and the joint loosens; this is why sprains mostly occur in plantarflexion.

questions.stem: Which statement about the sacroiliac joint is true?
options: It is a ball-and-socket joint allowing a wide range of movement.
It is a mixed joint: synovial in front, joined behind by strong interosseous ligaments.
It is not affected in ankylosing spondylitis.
It lies between the coccyx and the ilium.
It is an entirely fibrous joint.
questions.explanation: The part of the sacroiliac joint between the auricular surfaces is synovial; behind it are the interosseous sacroiliac ligaments, among the strongest in the body. It moves very little and transfers weight from the trunk to the pelvis. Ankylosing spondylitis usually begins at this joint (sacroiliitis).

questions.stem: What type of joint is the pubic symphysis?
questions.explanation: The two pubic bones meet by surfaces covered with hyaline cartilage through an intervening fibrocartilaginous disc (interpubic disc). In pregnancy the ligaments loosen under hormonal influence and the joint widens slightly.

questions.stem: Which statement about the openings formed by the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments is true?
options: They separate the muscular and vascular lacunae.
They convert the greater and lesser sciatic notches into the greater and lesser sciatic foramina.
They form the floor of the inguinal canal.
They form the wall of the pudendal canal.
questions.explanation: These two ligaments bind the sacrum to the ischium and stop the sacrum tipping forwards. They convert the greater sciatic notch into the greater sciatic foramen and the lesser notch into the lesser sciatic foramen. Piriformis divides the greater sciatic foramen into suprapiriform and infrapiriform parts.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a feature of a synovial joint?
options: Bone ends fused together by fibrous tissue
questions.explanation: In synovial joints the bone ends are covered with hyaline cartilage and separated by a joint cavity; the cavity is enclosed by the synovial membrane and fibrous capsule, and synovial fluid nourishes and lubricates it. Fusion by fibrous tissue is a feature of fibrous joints (sutures, syndesmoses).

questions.stem: What does Hilton's law state?
options: Each joint is supplied by a single nerve
The nerves supplying the muscles that move a joint also supply that joint and the skin over it
Articular cartilage is rich in nerves
A joint's ligaments act opposite to its muscles
A joint's blood supply comes only from the capsular arteries
questions.explanation: Hilton's law explains why joint pain can be referred to distant areas: for example, because the obturator nerve also supplies the hip joint, hip disease can cause pain on the inner side of the knee. Articular cartilage has no nerves or vessels.

questions.stem: What type of joint attaches the teeth to their sockets?
questions.explanation: A gomphosis is a type of fibrous joint: the tooth root is pegged into its alveolar socket by the periodontal ligament. Sutures join skull bones, a syndesmosis the distal tibia and fibula; the epiphyseal plate is a synchondrosis, and the pubic symphysis and intervertebral discs are symphyses.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a synchondrosis?
options: Joint between the 1st rib and manubrium
Y-shaped cartilage of the hip bone
questions.explanation: Synchondroses are primary cartilaginous joints formed by hyaline cartilage, and most ossify with time. The pubic symphysis is a secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis) containing a fibrocartilage disc; the intervertebral discs and manubriosternal joint also belong to this group.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: What movement mainly occurs at the atlanto-occipital joint?
options: Turning the head left and right (the 'no' movement)
Nodding the head forwards and backwards (the 'yes' movement)
questions.explanation: The occipital condyles sit on the superior articular facets of the atlas; this ellipsoid joint mainly allows flexion–extension and a little lateral bending. Most rotation occurs at the atlanto-axial joints.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: The nuchal ligament is the continuation in the neck of which ligament?
questions.explanation: The supraspinous ligament, joining the tips of the spinous processes, broadens above C7 into the triangular nuchal ligament extending to the external occipital protuberance; it provides attachment for trapezius and splenius.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: The tectorial membrane is the upward continuation of which ligament?
questions.explanation: The posterior longitudinal ligament broadens upwards from the body of the axis as the tectorial membrane and attaches to the clivus; it covers the dens and cruciform ligament from behind and protects the spinal cord.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: What are the components of the cruciform ligament of the atlas?
options: Transverse ligament of the atlas and longitudinal bands
Alar ligaments and apical ligament of the dens
questions.explanation: The horizontal limb of the cruciform ligament is the transverse ligament of the atlas, holding the dens against the anterior arch; its vertical limbs are longitudinal fibres running from the body of the axis to the foramen magnum. The alar ligaments run from the sides of the dens to the occipital condyles and limit rotation.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: Before intubation, a patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has flexion–extension neck X-rays; in flexion the distance between the atlas and dens increases markedly. Weakening of which ligament is chiefly responsible for this instability?
questions.explanation: Rheumatoid synovitis erodes the ligaments around the dens; when the transverse ligament loosens, the atlas slides forwards in flexion and the dens can compress the spinal cord. This is why neck flexion is avoided during intubation in RA patients.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: Which statement about the intervertebral disc is true?
options: There is also a disc between the atlas and axis
It makes up half the length of the spine
Its outer part is the fibrocartilaginous anulus fibrosus and its inner part the gelatinous nucleus pulposus
In adults the whole disc is well vascularised
questions.explanation: The discs are symphysis-type cartilaginous joints and make up about a quarter of the length of the spine. There is no disc between C1 and C2. In adults the disc is largely avascular and is nourished by diffusion from the end plates.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: What type of joint are the facet (zygapophysial) joints between the vertebrae?
questions.explanation: The facet joints between the superior and inferior articular processes are plane joints that allow gliding; the orientation of their surfaces determines the range of movement of each region (oblique in the neck, coronal in the thorax, sagittal in the lumbar spine). Their degeneration is a common cause of low back pain.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: In what order do movements occur at the temporomandibular joint when the mouth opens?
options: The condyle stays fixed behind the articular tubercle
The disc glides backwards independently of the condyle
First gliding in the upper compartment, then rotation in the lower compartment
First the condyle rotates like a hinge in the lower compartment, then the condyle and disc glide forwards together in the upper compartment
questions.explanation: The articular disc divides the TMJ into an upper (disc–fossa/tubercle) and a lower (disc–condyle) compartment. At the start of opening rotation occurs in the lower compartment; in wide opening the condyle–disc complex glides forwards towards the articular tubercle in the upper compartment (translation), driven by lateral pterygoid.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: With what tissue are the articular surfaces of the temporomandibular joint covered?
questions.explanation: The TMJ is an atypical synovial joint whose articular surfaces are covered with fibrocartilage, not hyaline cartilage; this relates to the intramembranous origin of the mandible. The joints at both ends of the clavicle show the same feature.

questions.stem: Which is the weakest part of the glenohumeral joint, and why?
options: The inferior part; there is no rotator cuff muscle or strong ligament support there
The anterior part; subscapularis is not present there
The superior part; there is no acromial support
The posterior part; the capsule is thinnest there
questions.explanation: The rotator cuff wraps the capsule above, in front and behind; the inferior part is protected only by the lax capsule and the inferior glenohumeral ligament. In abduction the humeral head escapes downwards and forwards through this area, putting the axillary nerve at risk.

questions.stem: What are the two parts of the coracoclavicular ligament?
questions.explanation: The coracoclavicular ligament is the strongest ligament suspending the clavicle from the scapula: it has a medial conoid part (to the conoid tubercle) and a lateral trapezoid part (to the trapezoid line). If it also tears in an AC dislocation, the clavicle rises markedly.

questions.stem: Which statement about the sternoclavicular joint is true?
options: It is a ball-and-socket joint without a disc
It is a uniaxial hinge joint
It is a saddle-type synovial joint containing an articular disc
questions.explanation: The sternoclavicular joint is the only true joint connecting the upper limb to the trunk; its articular disc divides it in two and acts as a strong cushion preventing the clavicle sliding medially. The costoclavicular ligament is the joint's main stabiliser.

questions.stem: Where is the triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) located?
options: At the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb
Between the radius and the scaphoid
Between the distal end of the ulna and the lunate and triquetrum
questions.explanation: The TFCC separates the ulnar head from the carpal bones, is the main stabiliser of the distal radio-ulnar joint and carries part of the load on the wrist. It can tear in a fall on the hand or with strain in ulnar deviation, causing pain on the ulnar side of the wrist.

questions.stem: Why is radial deviation (abduction) of the wrist more limited than ulnar deviation?
options: The ulna is longer than the radius
The radial styloid process extends further down
The TFCC is on the radial side
The ulnar collateral ligament of the wrist is weak
questions.explanation: The radial styloid process ends about 1 cm lower than the ulnar styloid and limits radial deviation by striking the scaphoid. Because the ulna does not articulate directly with the carpal bones, ulnar deviation is wider.

questions.stem: What type of joint are the proximal and distal radio-ulnar joints?
questions.explanation: Proximally the radial head rotates within the anular ligament, and distally the radius rotates around the ulnar head; together the two joints produce pronation and supination. The interosseous membrane between them is a syndesmosis.

questions.stem: What function does the direction of the fibres of the forearm interosseous membrane serve?
options: It transfers load from the hand and radius to the ulna
It transfers load from the ulna and radius to the hand
It replaces the collateral ligaments of the elbow
It only provides an origin for muscles
questions.explanation: At the wrist most of the load passes to the radius, at the elbow to the ulna (humero-ulnar joint). Because the membrane fibres run downwards and medially from the radius to the ulna, they transfer load from the radius to the ulna and provide a broad surface of origin for muscles.

questions.stem: What type of joint is the knee?
questions.explanation: The knee is a bicondylar joint between the two femoral condyles and the tibial plateaus that, in addition to hinge movement, allows some rotation in flexion; the patellofemoral joint lies within the same capsule.

questions.stem: Which movement does the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) mainly prevent?
options: Forward slide of the tibia on the femur
Backward slide of the tibia on the femur
questions.explanation: The ACL runs from the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia to the inner surface of the lateral femoral condyle; it limits forward slide of the tibia and excessive internal rotation. It is assessed with the anterior drawer and Lachman tests. Backward slide is limited by the PCL, valgus by the medial and varus by the lateral collateral ligament.
notes: This is the role of the medial patellofemoral ligament and VMO.
This is the role of the lateral collateral ligament.
This is the role of the posterior cruciate ligament.
This is the role of the medial collateral ligament.

questions.stem: In a motorcycle accident a patient takes a blow to the front of the upper tibia with the knee bent; with the knee at 90° of flexion the tibia can be pushed backwards relative to the femur. Which ligament is injured?
questions.explanation: The posterior cruciate ligament prevents the tibia sliding backwards; the 'dashboard injury' is the typical mechanism. The posterior drawer test and posterior sag of the tibia (sag sign) are positive. The PCL is thicker and stronger than the ACL.

questions.stem: What are the components of the classic 'unhappy triad' (O'Donoghue) knee injury?
options: Posterior cruciate ligament, lateral collateral ligament and lateral meniscus
Anterior cruciate ligament, posterior cruciate ligament and patellar ligament
Anterior cruciate ligament, medial collateral ligament and medial meniscus
Lateral collateral ligament, popliteus tendon and lateral meniscus
Medial collateral ligament, pes anserinus and medial meniscus
questions.explanation: A blow to the outer side of the knee with the foot fixed on the ground tears, through valgus and external rotation, the medial collateral ligament, then the medial meniscus attached to it and the anterior cruciate ligament. Recent studies show that the lateral meniscus is also often involved.

questions.stem: What happens during the locking of the knee in full extension (screw-home) with the foot on the ground?
options: The femur rotates laterally on the tibia
The tibia rotates medially on the femur
The femur rotates medially on the tibia
The patella slides upwards and locks
questions.explanation: Because the medial femoral condyle is longer, in the last degrees of extension in a closed chain the femur rotates medially and locks the joint; in an open chain the same movement appears as lateral rotation of the tibia. Popliteus unlocks it by rotating the femur laterally.

questions.stem: Which statement about the suprapatellar bursa is true?
options: It is always separate from the joint cavity
It lies between the patella and the skin
It lies between the patellar ligament and the tibia
It usually communicates with the knee joint cavity and swells with joint fluid
It lies beneath the pes anserinus
questions.explanation: The suprapatellar bursa lies beneath the quadriceps tendon in front of the femur and is like an upward extension of the joint cavity; in an effusion it swells above the patella. The prepatellar bursa lies in front of the patella, the deep infrapatellar bursa behind the patellar ligament.
notes: This describes the deep infrapatellar bursa.
This describes the pes anserinus bursa.

questions.stem: Which part of the menisci has no blood supply, so that tears heal poorly?
options: The ends of the posterior horns attached to the tibia
The edges attached to the capsule
The ends of the anterior horns attached to the tibia
The inner 2/3 facing into the joint (white zone)
The outer 1/3 near the capsule (red zone)
questions.explanation: The menisci are supplied peripherally by the perimeniscal capillary plexus; the outer third (red zone) is well vascularised and can be repaired, while the inner parts are nourished by diffusion from synovial fluid and their tears are usually resected.

questions.stem: A footballer feels sudden pain while twisting with the knee bent and foot planted. The next day he describes tenderness along the medial joint line and occasional catching and locking; McMurray's test is positive. What is the most likely injury?
questions.explanation: A loaded knee in flexion and rotation traps the meniscus between femur and tibia; joint-line tenderness, locking and McMurray's test suggest a meniscal tear. The medial meniscus, attached to the capsule and medial collateral ligament, is less mobile and tears more often.

questions.stem: What is the most stable (close-packed) position of the hip joint?
questions.explanation: In extension and internal rotation the iliofemoral, pubofemoral and ischiofemoral ligaments tighten spirally and press the femoral head firmly into the acetabulum. Flexion–adduction–internal rotation is the position most prone to posterior dislocation (dashboard injury).

questions.stem: Which fibrocartilaginous ring deepens the acetabulum?
options: Ligament of the head of the femur
questions.explanation: The acetabular labrum attaches to the rim of the acetabulum, its lower notch completed by the transverse acetabular ligament; it deepens the joint and holds the femoral head like a suction seal. It can tear in femoroacetabular impingement.

questions.stem: Which statement about the medial (deltoid) ligament of the ankle is true?
options: It consists of three separate bands and is the ligament most often torn
It fans out from the medial malleolus to the talus, calcaneus and navicular; it limits eversion
It runs between the tibia and fibula
It arises from the lateral malleolus
questions.explanation: The deltoid ligament is very strong; in forced eversion it often avulses the medial malleolus rather than tearing. The lateral ligament complex (ATFL, CFL, PTFL) is the structure most often injured in inversion sprains.

questions.stem: Which is the Lisfranc joint?
questions.explanation: The Lisfranc joint lies between the cuneiforms and cuboid and the metatarsal bases; the base of the 2nd metatarsal locks into the middle cuneiform and is the keystone of the joint. The talonavicular and calcaneocuboid joints together form the Chopart (transverse tarsal) joint.

questions.stem: What is the 'windlass' mechanism of the plantar fascia?
options: Dorsiflexion of the big toe tightens the plantar fascia and raises the medial arch
The fascia relaxes only when standing
The fascia tears and reattaches at heel strike
Plantarflexion of the big toe raises the arch
Ankle plantarflexion relaxes the fascia and flattens the arch
questions.explanation: The plantar fascia runs from the calcaneus to the bases of the toes; in push-off, when the big toe dorsiflexes, the fascia winds like a rope around the MTP joint, draws the heel and metatarsal heads together and raises the arch. The pain of the first morning steps in plantar fasciitis relates to this tension.

questions.stem: What does the plantar calcaneonavicular ('spring') ligament support?
options: The lower end of the fibula
The head of the talus and the medial longitudinal arch
questions.explanation: The spring ligament runs from the sustentaculum tali to the navicular and forms the floor of the socket in which the head of the talus sits; with the tibialis posterior tendon passing beneath it, it is the key support of the medial arch. Its laxity lets the head of the talus sink and causes flat foot.

questions.stem: What type of joint is the distal tibiofibular joint?
questions.explanation: The distal tibiofibular joint is a fibrous joint held by strong ligaments (anterior and posterior tibiofibular ligaments, interosseous ligament) and maintains the integrity of the ankle mortise. The proximal tibiofibular joint is a plane synovial joint.

questions.stem: A patient with an ankle sprain has tenderness and swelling over the medial malleolus; the ankle X-ray shows no fracture, but he also reports pain at the upper end of the fibula just below the knee. X-ray shows a proximal fibular fracture and widening of the tibiofibular space. What is this condition called?
questions.explanation: An external rotation force tears the deltoid ligament (or medial malleolus), travels up through the tibiofibular syndesmosis and interosseous membrane and fractures the proximal fibula. This is why the fibular head should never be left unexamined in ankle injuries.

questions.stem: Which ligament holds the sacroiliac joint together most strongly?
questions.explanation: The interosseous sacroiliac ligaments are short, very strong fibres behind the joint filling the space between the sacrum and the iliac tuberosity; they transfer body weight from the sacrum to the ilium. The anterior ligament is thin; the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments are accessory ligaments that stop the sacrum tipping forwards.

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT form part of the boundary of the pelvic outlet?
questions.explanation: The pelvic outlet is bounded in front by the pubic arch and lower border of the symphysis, at the sides by the ischial tuberosities and sacrotuberous ligaments, and behind by the tip of the coccyx. The promontory is the posterior boundary of the pelvic inlet.

questions.stem: In general, what do ligaments connect?
questions.explanation: Ligaments are bands of dense connective tissue joining bones together; they support the joint passively. The structure joining muscle to bone is a tendon.

questions.stem: What is the structure joining muscle to bone called?
questions.explanation: Tendons transmit muscle force to bone. Bursae are sacs that help tendons glide over bone; menisci and labra are intra-articular fibrocartilaginous structures.

questions.stem: What type of cartilage usually covers the articular surfaces of synovial joints?
questions.explanation: In most synovial joints the articular surfaces are covered by smooth hyaline cartilage. In a few joints, such as the temporomandibular and sternoclavicular joints, they are covered by fibrocartilage.

questions.stem: Which structure produces synovial fluid?
questions.explanation: The synovial membrane lining the inside of the joint capsule produces a slippery fluid rich in hyaluronic acid, which nourishes the cartilage and reduces friction.

questions.stem: What is the movement that decreases the angle between two bones (bending) called?
questions.explanation: Flexion is bending and extension straightening (increasing the angle). Abduction moves away from the midline, adduction towards it, and rotation turns a part about its own axis.

questions.stem: What is the movement of raising the arm sideways away from the body called?
questions.explanation: Abduction is moving a limb away from the midline of the body; at the shoulder it is produced mainly by supraspinatus and deltoid.

questions.stem: What is the forearm movement that turns the palm upwards (forwards) called?
questions.explanation: In supination the palm faces up/forwards, in pronation down/backwards; these movements take place at the radio-ulnar joints. Inversion and eversion are movements of the foot.

questions.stem: What is the movement that turns the sole of the foot inwards called?
questions.explanation: In inversion the sole turns inwards, in eversion outwards. These movements take place mainly at the subtalar and transverse tarsal joints; most ankle sprains occur in inversion.

questions.stem: Which is the most mobile joint of the body?
questions.explanation: The shoulder trades stability for a wide range of movement: the humeral head contacts the shallow glenoid only partly. It is therefore the large joint that dislocates most often.

questions.stem: Which is the largest joint of the body?
questions.explanation: The knee, formed by the femur, tibia and patella, is the largest and most complex synovial joint of the body.

questions.stem: Which bones take part in the knee joint?
questions.explanation: The knee consists of the tibiofemoral and patellofemoral joints. The fibula does not take part in the knee joint; the superior tibiofibular joint is a separate joint.

questions.stem: Between which bones is the shoulder joint?
questions.explanation: The glenohumeral joint lies between the head of the humerus and the glenoid cavity of the scapula. The clavicle and scapula form the acromioclavicular joint.

questions.stem: What type of joint is the hip joint?
questions.explanation: The hip joint is a ball-and-socket joint between the femoral head and the acetabulum; it moves in three axes and, thanks to its deep socket, is more stable than the shoulder.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: Between which bones is the jaw (temporomandibular) joint?
questions.explanation: The temporomandibular joint lies between the condyle of the mandible and the mandibular fossa and articular tubercle of the temporal bone; it contains a fibrocartilaginous disc.

questions.stem: Between which bones is the pubic symphysis?
questions.explanation: The pubic symphysis is the fibrocartilaginous joint joining the two pubic bones in the midline in front; the interpubic disc lies between them.

questions.stem: In which joint are the menisci found?
questions.explanation: The medial and lateral menisci lie between the femoral and tibial condyles in the knee; they improve congruence and distribute load.

questions.stem: What is a bursa?
options: A small fluid-filled sac lined by synovial membrane between structures that rub together
A fibrocartilaginous disc inside a joint
The outer layer of articular cartilage
A band joining muscle to bone
questions.explanation: Bursae reduce friction between structures that rub against each other, such as tendon and bone or skin and bone. Their inflammation from repeated pressure or friction is called bursitis.

questions.stem: How is articular cartilage nourished?
options: By capillaries from the bone marrow
By diffusion from the synovial fluid
questions.explanation: Articular cartilage has no vessels, nerves or perichondrium; nutrients come by diffusion from the synovial fluid. That is why cartilage damage does not heal on its own.

questions.stem: In rheumatoid arthritis, what is the inflammatory tissue that erodes articular cartilage and bone called?
questions.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis is chronic inflammation of the synovial membrane; the thickened synovium, called pannus, erodes cartilage and bone. Osteophytes are a sign of osteoarthritis, tophi of gout.

questions.stem: In people who work kneeling, swelling in front of the kneecap is a bursitis of which bursa?
questions.explanation: Prepatellar bursitis ('housemaid's knee') is inflammation of the bursa between the patella and the skin from repeated pressure. Infrapatellar bursitis ('clergyman's knee') lies in front of the tibial tuberosity.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: What is the main function of the alar ligaments?
options: To prevent excessive flexion of the head
To press the dens against the anterior arch of the atlas
To limit excessive rotation of the head
To join the posterior arch of the atlas to the occiput
To form the anterior wall of the vertebral canal
questions.explanation: The alar ligaments run from the sides of the dens to the occipital condyles and prevent excessive turning of the head at the atlanto-axial joint. The ligament pressing the dens against the anterior arch is the transverse ligament of the atlas.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: Why is rotation of the spine limited in the lumbar region?
options: Because the facet joint surfaces lie in the sagittal plane
Because the discs are very thin
Because there is no ligamentum flavum
questions.explanation: The orientation of the facet joints determines the type of movement in each region: lumbar facets are sagittal and allow flexion-extension but restrict rotation; thoracic facets lie in the frontal plane and rotation is free.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: In which vertebrae are the uncovertebral (Luschka) joints found?
questions.explanation: Uncovertebral joints are cleft-like joints between the uncinate processes on the upper lateral margins of the C3–C7 bodies and the vertebra above; their osteophytes can narrow the intervertebral foramen.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: Which ligament prevents backward displacement of the condyle at the jaw joint?
questions.explanation: The lateral ligament is a thickening of the outer side of the capsule; it runs from the zygomatic arch to the neck of the mandible and prevents the condyle from moving backwards and downwards. The spheno- and stylomandibular ligaments are accessory ligaments away from the capsule.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: What is the respiratory movement of the lower ribs that increases the transverse diameter of the chest called?
questions.explanation: The lower ribs rise upwards and outwards at their middle like a bucket handle and increase the transverse diameter. The pump-handle movement of the upper ribs increases the anteroposterior diameter.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: Which of the following ribs does NOT articulate with a transverse process (costotransverse joint)?
questions.explanation: The costotransverse joint lies between the tubercle of the rib and the transverse process. The 11th and 12th ribs have no tubercle and do not form this joint.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: Which movement increases the anteroposterior diameter of the pelvic outlet during childbirth?
questions.explanation: The sacrococcygeal joint lets the coccyx move backwards during childbirth, increasing the anteroposterior diameter of the pelvic outlet by a few centimetres.

questions.stem: Which ligament mainly provides stability of the sternoclavicular joint?
questions.explanation: The costoclavicular ligament, joining the medial end of the clavicle to the first costal cartilage, is the strongest stabiliser of the joint and limits elevation of the clavicle.

questions.stem: Which structures form the coracoacromial arch?
options: Acromion, clavicle and spine of the scapula
Greater tubercle, lesser tubercle and transverse humeral ligament
Acromion, coracoacromial ligament and coracoid process
questions.explanation: The coracoacromial arch forms a protective roof over the humeral head; the supraspinatus tendon and subacromial bursa pass beneath it. Impingement syndrome occurs under this arch.

questions.stem: Which ligament holds the tendon of the long head of biceps in the intertubercular groove?
questions.explanation: The transverse humeral ligament spans the greater and lesser tubercles and turns the groove into a canal. If it tears, the tendon can slip out of the groove with a painful click.

questions.stem: What is the anteroinferior labral tear that is the main cause of recurrent anterior shoulder dislocation called?
questions.explanation: A Bankart lesion is detachment of the anteroinferior labrum and inferior glenohumeral ligament from the glenoid. Hill–Sachs is an impaction fracture of the posterolateral humeral head; SLAP is a superior labral tear.

questions.stem: Which part of the labrum does a SLAP lesion involve?
options: The superior labrum (where the long head of biceps attaches)
questions.explanation: A SLAP (Superior Labrum Anterior to Posterior) lesion is a front-to-back tear of the superior labrum where the long head of biceps attaches; it is common in throwing sports.

questions.stem: Which is the most important structure for valgus stability of the elbow?
options: Anterior band of the ulnar collateral ligament
questions.explanation: The anterior band of the medial (ulnar) collateral ligament protects the elbow against valgus force. In throwing athletes a tear of this band is reconstructed with a tendon graft ('Tommy John' surgery).

questions.stem: What is the ligament tear that most often causes wrist instability, and its radiographic sign?
options: Pisohamate ligament – fracture of the hook of hamate
Ulnar collateral ligament – dislocation of the ulnar head
Radial collateral ligament – fracture of the radial styloid
Lunotriquetral ligament – dorsal rotation of the lunate
Scapholunate ligament – gap wider than 3 mm between scaphoid and lunate
questions.explanation: In a scapholunate ligament tear the AP radiograph shows a gap between the two bones (Terry Thomas sign) and a ring sign of the scaphoid; untreated, it leads to DISI deformity and SLAC arthritis.

questions.stem: What is osteoarthritis of the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb called?
questions.explanation: Rhizarthrosis is osteoarthritis of the saddle joint between the trapezium and the 1st metacarpal; it causes pain on gripping and turning a key, especially in postmenopausal women.

questions.stem: If the hand is to be splinted for a long time, why are the MCP joints kept in flexion?
options: Tendons are better nourished in flexion.
Nerves are freed from pressure in flexion.
Bones do not unite in extension.
The collateral ligaments are taut in flexion, so they do not shorten and cause stiffness.
The volar plate relaxes and heals in flexion.
questions.explanation: Because of the cam shape of the metacarpal head, the MCP collateral ligaments are taut in flexion. If the joint is held in extension for long, the slack ligaments shorten and a permanent extension contracture develops.

questions.stem: Skier's thumb (gamekeeper's thumb) is an injury of which ligament?
options: Volar plate of the thumb IP joint
Ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb MCP joint
Radial collateral ligament of the thumb MCP joint
Anterior oblique ligament of the thumb CMC joint
questions.explanation: Forced abduction of the thumb when falling onto a ski pole tears the ulnar collateral ligament of the MCP joint; grip and pinch strength are reduced.

questions.stem: Which structure prevents hyperextension at the PIP joints of the fingers?
questions.explanation: The volar plate is a thick fibrocartilaginous plate on the palmar side of the joint and limits hyperextension. Its avulsion in a hyperextension injury can lead to a swan-neck deformity.

questions.stem: Which ligament prevents excessive abduction of the hip joint?
options: Ligament of the head of the femur
questions.explanation: The pubofemoral ligament runs from the superior pubic ramus to the inferior-anterior capsule and limits excessive abduction. The iliofemoral ligament prevents hyperextension, the ischiofemoral excessive internal rotation.

questions.stem: The oblique popliteal ligament is an expansion of the tendon of which muscle?
questions.explanation: The oblique popliteal ligament runs upwards and laterally from the semimembranosus tendon and reinforces the posterior knee capsule; it lies just in front of the popliteal artery.

questions.stem: Which tendon passes between the lateral (fibular) collateral ligament and the lateral meniscus of the knee?
options: Tendon of the lateral head of gastrocnemius
questions.explanation: The lateral collateral ligament is separate from the capsule and the lateral meniscus, and the popliteus tendon passes between them. The lateral meniscus is therefore more mobile and tears less often than the medial one.

questions.stem: Which lateral ankle ligament is the strongest and tears least often?
questions.explanation: The lateral ligaments tear in sequence from front to back: first the anterior talofibular, then the calcaneofibular. The posterior talofibular is the strongest and tears only in severe injuries.

questions.stem: Which ligament does the anterior drawer test of the ankle mainly assess?
questions.explanation: In the anterior drawer test the tibia is fixed and the heel pulled forwards; forward sliding of the talus indicates a tear of the anterior talofibular ligament. The calcaneofibular ligament is assessed with the talar tilt (inversion stress) test.

questions.stem: Which structures are injured in a high ankle sprain?
options: Lateral collateral ligaments of the ankle
questions.explanation: A high ankle sprain usually occurs with external rotation and tears the syndesmotic ligaments joining the tibia and fibula; it takes much longer to heal than a lateral ligament sprain.

questions.stem: Which structure, located in the sinus tarsi, is the strongest ligament of the subtalar joint?
questions.explanation: The interosseous talocalcaneal ligament lies in the sinus tarsi between the talus and calcaneus and is the main ligament of the subtalar joint.

questions.stem: Which joints make up Chopart's (transverse tarsal) joint?
questions.explanation: Chopart's joint is the S-shaped joint line between the hindfoot and midfoot and is one of the amputation levels. Lisfranc's joint is the tarsometatarsal joints.

questions.stem: Where does the Lisfranc ligament run?
options: From the navicular to the medial cuneiform
From the calcaneus to the cuboid
From the intermediate cuneiform to the base of the 2nd metatarsal
From the cuboid to the base of the 5th metatarsal
From the medial cuneiform to the base of the 2nd metatarsal
questions.explanation: The Lisfranc ligament is a strong interosseous ligament between the medial cuneiform and the base of the 2nd metatarsal; since there is no ligament between the bases of the 1st and 2nd metatarsals, it is the key to the tarsometatarsal joint.

questions.stem: Which bone is the keystone of the lateral longitudinal arch of the foot?
questions.explanation: The keystone of the medial longitudinal arch is the head of the talus, that of the lateral arch the cuboid. The lateral arch is low and close to the ground.

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of acquired flatfoot in adults?
questions.explanation: Tibialis posterior is the most important dynamic support of the medial arch; degeneration and failure of its tendon lead to collapse of the medial arch and valgus of the heel.

questions.stem: A patient who fell onto a plantarflexed foot has midfoot swelling and plantar ecchymosis; the radiograph shows a gap between the bases of the 1st and 2nd metatarsals. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Plantar ecchymosis and a gap between the 1st and 2nd metatarsal bases are typical signs of a Lisfranc ligament injury; about one in five is missed at first presentation, so it needs careful assessment.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: Which type of dens fracture has the highest risk of non-union?
options: Type III (extending into the body of the axis)
questions.explanation: In the Anderson–D'Alonzo classification a type II fracture crosses the base of the dens; non-union is frequent in this poorly vascularised region. Type III extends into the body of the axis and usually heals.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: Where does the sensory innervation of the facet (zygapophyseal) joints come from?
options: Anterior rami of the spinal nerves
Medial branches of the posterior rami of the spinal nerves
Lateral branches of the posterior rami
questions.explanation: Each facet joint is supplied by the medial branches of the posterior rami of two adjacent levels. In facet pain these branches are targeted with blocks or radiofrequency ablation.

questions.group: Joints of the skull and spine
questions.stem: The sphenomandibular ligament is a remnant of which pharyngeal arch structure?
options: Cartilage of the 1st pharyngeal arch (Meckel's cartilage)
questions.explanation: Meckel's cartilage gives rise to the malleus, incus and sphenomandibular ligament. Reichert's cartilage (2nd arch) forms the stapes, styloid process and stylohyoid ligament.

questions.stem: Which forearm ligament has fibres running in the opposite direction to those of the interosseous membrane?
questions.explanation: Fibres of the interosseous membrane run downwards and medially from radius to ulna, whereas the oblique cord descends laterally from the ulnar tuberosity to the radius. It supports the proximal radio-ulnar joint.

questions.stem: What is the ligament-poor area on the palmar side of the capitate, through which perilunate dislocations occur, called?
questions.explanation: The space of Poirier is the weak area between the radioscaphocapitate and radiolunate ligaments; in perilunate dislocation the capitate separates from the lunate here.

questions.stem: Tears in which part of the TFCC do not heal because it is avascular, and require debridement?
questions.explanation: Only the outer margin of the TFCC is well vascularised. Central tears do not heal and are treated by arthroscopic debridement, whereas peripheral tears are repaired.

questions.stem: Which condition, seen in people whose ulna is longer than the radius (ulnar positive variance), causes wear of the TFCC and lunate?
questions.explanation: In ulnar positive variance the ulnar head presses on the TFCC and lunate, causing ulnar-sided pain and cartilage damage of the lunate. Kienböck disease is associated rather with ulnar negative variance.

questions.stem: Which is the most important stabilising ligament of the thumb carpometacarpal joint?
questions.explanation: The anterior oblique ligament runs from the tubercle of the trapezium to the anteromedial base of the 1st metacarpal; it is also the ligament that holds the small medial fragment in place in a Bennett fracture.

questions.stem: In a Stener lesion, which structure becomes interposed between the torn ulnar collateral ligament and its attachment?
questions.explanation: When the ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb MCP joint ruptures, its end may come to lie on top of the adductor aponeurosis; the interposed aponeurosis prevents healing, so surgery is needed.

questions.stem: Which structure dislocates in a Monteggia fracture?
options: Head of the radius (proximal radio-ulnar joint)
questions.explanation: In a Monteggia fracture a fracture of the proximal third of the ulna is accompanied by dislocation of the radial head. In a Galeazzi fracture a radial shaft fracture is accompanied by dislocation of the distal radio-ulnar joint.

questions.stem: Why is posterior dislocation of the sternoclavicular joint an emergency?
options: The medial end of the clavicle can compress the great vessels and trachea behind it.
It also dislocates the shoulder joint.
questions.explanation: In posterior dislocation the medial end of the clavicle can compress the brachiocephalic vessels, trachea and oesophagus; unlike anterior dislocation, it may therefore need urgent reduction.

questions.stem: How much of the posterior surface of the femoral neck does the hip joint capsule enclose?
options: All of it up to the greater trochanter
questions.explanation: Anteriorly the capsule reaches the intertrochanteric line and encloses the whole neck; posteriorly it covers only the medial 2/3 of the neck. Femoral neck fractures are therefore largely intracapsular.

questions.stem: Which ligament limits excessive internal rotation of the hip joint?
options: Ligament of the head of the femur
questions.explanation: The ischiofemoral ligament spirals from the ischium onto the posterior capsule; it is taut in internal rotation and extension.

questions.stem: Which is the most important static stabiliser of the posterolateral corner of the knee?
questions.explanation: The posterolateral corner consists of the lateral collateral ligament, popliteus tendon, popliteofibular ligament and capsule; the popliteofibular ligament is the main static restraint to external rotation.

questions.stem: In the dial test, increased external rotation at both 30° and 90° of knee flexion suggests what?
options: An isolated medial collateral ligament tear
Combined injury of the posterolateral corner and posterior cruciate ligament
An isolated anterior cruciate ligament tear
questions.explanation: Increased external rotation only at 30° suggests an isolated posterolateral corner injury; at both 30° and 90°, a combined injury of the posterolateral corner and PCL.

questions.stem: Which lateral ankle ligament contributes to both the talocrural and subtalar joints?
questions.explanation: The calcaneofibular ligament runs from the lateral malleolus to the calcaneus and thus crosses both joints; it is assessed with the talar tilt test.

questions.stem: Which is the most important structure preventing lateral shift of the talus within the ankle mortise?
options: Deep (tibiotalar) part of the deltoid ligament
Tibionavicular part of the deltoid ligament
questions.explanation: The deep tibiotalar fibres of the deltoid ligament bind the talus to the medial malleolus; if they tear, the talus shifts laterally, the joint contact area decreases and osteoarthritis develops.

questions.stem: From the calcaneus, to which bones do the two limbs of the bifurcate ligament run?
questions.explanation: The calcaneonavicular and calcaneocuboid limbs of the Y-shaped bifurcate ligament lie on the dorsum of Chopart's joint; its sprain causes pain in front of the sinus tarsi.

questions.stem: What is the typical sign of talocalcaneal coalition on a lateral ankle radiograph?
questions.explanation: In talocalcaneal coalition a continuous C-shaped contour forms between the dome of the talus and the sustentaculum tali. In calcaneonavicular coalition the oblique view shows the 'anteater nose'.

questions.stem: A skier who twisted the knee into external rotation reports sudden pain and instability; after ACL reconstruction, external rotation instability of the knee persists. Which injury may have been missed?
options: Posterolateral corner injury of the knee
questions.explanation: Posterolateral corner injuries often accompany cruciate ligament injuries; if they are not recognised and repaired, the cruciate graft is overloaded and the reconstruction fails.
